row: | DOC-A.1-74 | **Figurative constant values — representation of ZERO, SPACE and QUOTE**, §8.3.3.6 (§8.3.3.6.4 GR1), required + documented | Each has ONE representation, the same code unit in both coded character sets (both are UTF-16, one code unit per character position — item 33): **SPACE is U+0020, ZERO is U+0030 (the character '0'), QUOTE is U+0022 (the character '"')**. In an alphanumeric item that is the one-byte DISPLAY image 0x20 / 0x30 / 0x22 (item 209); in a national item it is the two-byte code unit 0x0020 / 0x0030 / 0x0022 (two bytes per national position, as item 209's row states). So `MOVE SPACE` to a `PIC X` item gives `FUNCTION ORD` 33, ZERO 49, QUOTE 35, and the national item holds the same values; `SPACE = X"20"`, `QUOTE = X"22"`, `ZERO = X"30"` and `QUOTE = NX"0022"` are all true. Neither a PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE, an ALPHABET clause nor a CODE-SET clause changes these values in storage; those clauses affect comparison order and the file's external code set only. The single source for the fill characters is `FigurativeConstants.FillChar`. (A BOOLEAN receiver is outside this item: ZERO fills it with the boolean character '0', and so does SPACE, determination D-B2 in §3.) | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-95 | **Hexadecimal alphanumeric literals — result when no corresponding character exists**, §8.3.3.2 GR4 (printed as §8.3.3.2.4 GR5 in this text), required + documented | **The case does not arise: every hex-character-sequence has a corresponding character.** A hexadecimal alphanumeric literal takes TWO hexadecimal digits per character (§8.3.3.2.3 SR6; any other count is refused, COBOLNET1635), and the group `hh` is the character whose code is U+00hh, which is also its one-byte DISPLAY image (item 209). All 256 values 00 through FF are characters of the alphanumeric set, so each group is stored as that character, including the control codes 00–1F, 7F and 80–9F, with no diagnostic and no exception condition. Example: `X"80FF0041"` is four characters whose `FUNCTION ORD` values are 129, 256, 1 and 66. What a device shows for a control character on DISPLAY is the device's business, not the literal's. Implemented in `CobolLiteral.DecodeHex`. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-97 | **Hexadecimal national literals — result when no corresponding character exists**, §8.3.3.5 GR4 (printed as §8.3.3.5.4 GR5 in this text), required + documented | A hexadecimal national literal takes FOUR hexadecimal digits per character (§8.3.3.5.3 SR5; any other count is refused, COBOLNET1635), and each group is stored **verbatim as that UTF-16 code unit**, the national character representation (item 33). A group that is not a character on its own, such as a surrogate half D800–DFFF or a noncharacter such as FFFE or FFFF, is stored unchanged, as one character position, with no diagnostic and no exception condition. It then behaves as any other national character: `FUNCTION LENGTH(NX"D800")` is 1, `FUNCTION ORD` gives the code plus 1 (55297 for D800, 65536 for FFFF), and comparison uses the code unit's value. Two groups that form a valid surrogate pair stay two character positions. On DISPLAY to a UTF-8 device, an unpaired surrogate is written as U+FFFD. Implemented in `CobolLiteral.DecodeHexGroups`. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-94 | **GOBACK statement — constraints on the value in the STATUS phrase**, §14.9.18.3 GR10 (printed as §14.9.18.4 GR10 in this text), required + documented | **No value is refused. The STATUS operand becomes the process exit code**, with the same mapping as STOP (A.1 item 192, §3 'STOP RUN / GOBACK termination status'). The syntax rules still apply: identifier-2 must be an integer data item or a data item of usage display or national (§14.9.18.3 SR6), and a numeric literal-1 must be an integer (SR7). The mapping is: **(1)** a numeric operand's integer value is the exit code (a data item's value truncated toward zero); **(2)** a non-numeric operand (an alphanumeric or national item, a non-numeric literal, a figurative constant) is decoded as an unsigned integer from its digit characters, and a position that is not a digit adds no digit, so `STATUS "007"` exits 7, `STATUS "A1B2"` exits 12 and `STATUS "ABEND"` or `STATUS SPACE` exits 0 (`CobolNum.FromAlphanumeric`); **(3)** the host then keeps what it can report: the value is narrowed to a 32-bit integer and a POSIX host keeps only the low 8 bits, so `STATUS 300` exits 44 and `STATUS -3` exits 253. With no STATUS value, `GOBACK WITH ERROR` exits 1 and `WITH NORMAL` (or no phrase) exits 0; a STATUS value, when present, wins over ERROR or NORMAL. The value reaches the operating system only when the GOBACK ends the run unit, that is, in a main program (§14.9.18.4 GR3); in a called program the GOBACK returns to its caller and the status is not used. The phrase is COBOL-2023 only: at `--std 2014` and below it is refused with COBOLNET0900. Implemented by `CallBinder.DecodeGobackPhrases` and the `RunUnit.ExitStatus` setter. | `conformance-test:StopGobackExitCodeTests.TerminationStatus_SetsProcessExitCode`; `conformance-test:StopGobackExitCodeTests.NonNumericStatusOperand_IsLegalAndInterpretedNumerically` |

row: | DOC-A.1-78 | **Fixed file attributes — whether the ability to share a physical file is a fixed file attribute**, §9.1.6, required + documented | **No.** A physical file records nothing about sharing. The sharing mode belongs to each FILE CONNECTOR: it comes from that connector's SHARING clause, or from the SHARING phrase of the OPEN that opens it (§14.9.27.4 GR21–GR23). It is set when the OPEN succeeds and checked against the connectors that have the same physical file open at that moment (§9.1.15 Table 19). When the connector is closed, its sharing mode is gone. So a file created through a `SHARING WITH NO OTHER` connector can later be opened through two `SHARING WITH ALL OTHER` connectors at once, and both OPENs succeed with 00. While the NO OTHER connector is open, any other OPEN of the file fails with 61, and the NO OTHER connector's own OPEN fails with 61 while other connectors have the file open. This is also why A.1 item 129's validated fixed attributes never include sharing. Implemented by `FileRegistry.RegisterSharing` (the per-connector mode) and `FileRegistry.SharedOpenAttempt` (the check at OPEN). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-76 | **File sharing — which devices allow concurrent access to a physical file**, §9.1.15, required + documented | **All of them.** Every physical file is a path in the host file system: a regular file, or a device path such as `/dev/null` that the host opens as a file. The device classes `DISK` and `PRINTER` both name such a file (item 71). COBOL.NET treats every physical file as one that allows concurrent access, so it is *shareable* in the sense of §14.9.27.4 GR21 and the SHARING clause and SHARING phrase always apply. A second connector's OPEN of the same file is decided by §9.1.15 Table 19: connectors that both specify `SHARING WITH ALL OTHER` (with `LOCK MODE MANUAL`) can be open on one regular file or on `/dev/null` at the same time, each with status 00, and a `SHARING WITH NO OTHER` OPEN of a file another connector has open fails with 61. `ASSIGN TO PRINTER "f"` and `ASSIGN TO DISK "f"` are the same shareable file. This row covers only which files can be shared. How strongly the file lock excludes other run units depends on the host, and that is open under kb/Work PB833. The mode used when no sharing mode is specified (item 77) is open under kb/Work PB322. Implemented by `FileRegistry.SharedOpenAttempt` and `PhysicalFileTable`, which apply Table 19 to every connector without testing the device. | — |

Probe /tmp/adj/doc/doc-w1-s3/probe/d76.cob: ASSIGN PRINTER "d76.prt" OUTPUT 00 plus ASSIGN DISK "d76.prt" EXTEND 00 concurrently (ALL OTHER), both writes land; two ALL OTHER EXTEND on /dev/null 00/00, NO OTHER on it while they are open 61, alone 00. sh78.cob confirms the regular-file arbitration. row: | DOC-A.1-72 | **FILE-CONTROL entry, ASSIGN clause — consistency rules for external file connectors**, §12.4.5 GR1, required + documented | §12.4.5.3 GR1 b) requires the file control entries that reference one external file connector to have *"A consistent specification for data-name-1, device-name-1, and literal-1 in the ASSIGN clause"* and leaves the rules to the implementor. **COBOL.NET's rule: the entries must name the same file target and the same data-name-1, and nothing more.** (1) **The TO phrase is compared by the file name it resolves to** under item 71's rule, not by the words written. A leading device class is not part of the name, so `ASSIGN TO DISK "xa.dat"`, `ASSIGN TO PRINTER "xa.dat"` and `ASSIGN TO "xa.dat"` are consistent. A device-name and a literal with the same spelling are the same name, so `ASSIGN TO XADAT` and `ASSIGN TO "xadat"` are consistent. The comparison ignores case, so `"Data.txt"` and `"data.txt"` are consistent, even though on a case-sensitive host they name different physical files; the file opened is the one named in the program that executes the OPEN. An entry with a TO phrase and one without are not consistent. (2) **The USING data-name-1 is compared by spelling, qualifiers included, ignoring case.** `IN` and `OF` are the same, so `FNAME IN G` and `FNAME OF G` are consistent; `FNAME` and `FNAME OF G` are not, and neither are an entry with a USING phrase and one without. The check runs only when checking for EC-EXTERNAL-FILE-MISMATCH is enabled. It happens when a second program that describes the external file is activated: the two ASSIGN fields are part of the `SelectFingerprint` each program registers with `ExternalStore.Describe` (built in `OoEmitter.EmitExternalDescribes`), and a difference raises **EC-EXTERNAL-FILE-MISMATCH** (§14.8.4.4), which is fatal. **⛔ The two programs still hold SEPARATE STORAGE for an identically-spelled data-name-1, and that is deliberate.** §12.4.5.3 GR3 b) associates the connector with the file named *"in the runtime element that executes the OPEN, SORT, or MERGE statement"*, which only makes sense if the entries MAY name different data items. GR1 i) shows how the standard words it when it wants the opposite (FILE STATUS: *"where data-name-4 shall reference the same corresponding external data item"*), and §13.4.5.4 GR2 c) 2. does the same for LINAGE; GR1 b) says neither. Implemented at `FileConnector.Associate`, called with the executing program's own rendered specification (kb/Work PB673). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-69 | **Fatal exception conditions — which are detected at compile time, and when**, §14.6.13.1.3, optional + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY) | **One fatal exception condition is detected at compile time: EC-ORDER-NOT-SUPPORTED.** When a SPECIAL-NAMES `ORDER TABLE ... IS literal` clause names a cultural ordering table this implementation does not provide, the compiler reports **warning COBOLNET1662** at that clause. A FUNCTION STANDARD-COMPARE that uses the table sets EC-ORDER-NOT-SUPPORTED at run time (§15.85.4). **The compiler always produces executable code**, whether checking is enabled or not. The permission §14.6.13.1.3 gives to omit code for a condition detected at compile time is never used, so detection never becomes a compile error. Nothing else is detected at compile time. A constant subscript outside the OCCURS bounds, a constant reference modification outside the item, a literal zero divisor and a constant intrinsic argument outside its domain all compile without a diagnostic. These are general rules, not syntax rules. With checking enabled the program ends at run time with the fatal condition (EC-BOUND-SUBSCRIPT, EC-BOUND-REF-MOD, EC-SIZE-ZERO-DIVIDE, EC-ARGUMENT-FUNCTION); with checking off it continues. Compile-time errors that name a run-time condition, such as COBOLNET1688 for EC-PROGRAM-ARG-MISMATCH, enforce syntax rules and are not detections under this item. The warning is `DiagnosticCatalog.OrderTableUnresolved`. | — |

record.notes: VOLUNTARY row: A.1 69 is optional and need not be documented. §14.6.13.1.3 8) (cite.py OK). All 17 Warning descriptors in DiagnosticCatalog were scanned; only COBOLNET1662 (order-table-unresolved) anticipates a fatal EC (EC-ORDER-NOT-SUPPORTED, L3 Fatal in ExceptionCatalog). row: | DOC-A.1-100 | **Implementor-defined level-2 exception conditions, EC-level-2-IMP — specification and meaning of each specified level-2 IMP exception condition**, §14.6.13.1.6 Table 13 (§14.6.13.1.1, the '-IMP' suffix type), optional + documented if provided | **Provided: 20 of Table 13's 22 EC-level-2-IMP names are valid exception-names, and each is FATAL.** The names are EC-ARGUMENT-IMP, EC-BOUND-IMP, EC-CONTINUE-IMP, EC-DATA-IMP, EC-EXTERNAL-IMP, EC-FLOW-IMP, EC-FUNCTION-IMP, EC-I-O-IMP, EC-LOCALE-IMP, EC-MCS-IMP, EC-OO-IMP, EC-ORDER-IMP, EC-OVERFLOW-IMP, EC-PROGRAM-IMP, EC-RAISING-IMP, EC-RANGE-IMP, EC-REPORT-IMP, EC-SCREEN-IMP, EC-SIZE-IMP, EC-SORT-MERGE-IMP, EC-STORAGE-IMP and EC-VALIDATE-IMP. EC-CONTINUE-IMP, EC-EXTERNAL-IMP and EC-MCS-IMP are COBOL-2023 names; below 2023 they are refused with COBOLNET0878. EC-SCREEN-IMP and EC-VALIDATE-IMP belong to the screen and VALIDATE modules, which this implementation does not provide (Annex A.4.2, A.4.14). They are refused wherever they are written, with COBOLNET1707 and COBOLNET1710. The other 20 can be used in `>>TURN`, `RAISE EXCEPTION` and wherever an exception-name is allowed. Table 13 leaves their fatality to the implementor (Imp), and this implementation treats every one as fatal. An unhandled one ends the run unit abnormally, and so does a `RAISE EXCEPTION` of one with checking not enabled. **Meaning: the implementation itself sets only EC-PROGRAM-IMP**, and only when a contained program is activated while the program that contains it has no instance (an internal consistency failure of the program table, reported as 'internal: contained program ... activated while its container is not instantiated'). The implementation never sets any of the others, so a program sees them only when it raises them itself. EC-I-O-IMP is Table 13's 'I-O status 9x' condition, but the only 9x status COBOL.NET defines, '90', carries EC-I-O-LINAGE instead (item 110). EC-RAISING-IMP is never set at run time either. The names and fatality are `ExceptionCatalog` (EcFatality.Imp); the one raise site is `ProgramTable.ParentInstance`, through the default exception-name of `CobolCallException`. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-79 | **FLAG-02 directive — the warning mechanism**, §7.3.14 GR1 (§7.3.14.4 GR1), required + documented | **A compile-time warning, COBOLNET1620, for each flagged construct. The warning does not change the compiled program.** `>>FLAG-02` names ALL, or one or more of its five options (EC-PROGRAM-EXCEPTIONS, I-O-STATUS-07, MOVE-TO-SAME-NAME, RANGE-EXCEPTION-FOR-INDEX, TERMINATE-WITH-VARYING) in any order, followed by ON or OFF. If ON and OFF are both omitted, ON applies. An option is on from the line after the directive until a later FLAG-02 turns it off, or turns ALL off, or the compilation group ends. Every option is off by default. While an option is on, each construct §7.3.14.4 GR4 describes for it is reported as `warning COBOLNET1620: <the construct> (<the 2002-to-2014 change>) — flagged by >>FLAG-02 <option>` at the construct's line and column. For example, with I-O-STATUS-07 on, each `CLOSE ... WITH NO REWIND` or `UNIT` is reported. An option word that is not one of the five, or ALL combined with named options, is refused with COBOLNET1622. The directive is a COBOL-2014 element: at `--std 2002` and below it is refused with COBOLNET0900, and at `--std 2023` it still works but draws the obsolete-element warning COBOLNET0903 (§7.3.14.1 NOTE). Known defects in the open notes, not part of this determination: the EC-PROGRAM-EXCEPTIONS warnings have no source location and are reported once per program (kb/Work PB1376), and some GR4 construct populations are narrower than the rule (kb/Work PB1375). record.notes: Not recorded this round. The item's two arms are §7.3.9.3 2) a) and b) (cite.py OK). Arm b) is defective: no call-convention-name is defined, yet any word is accepted and the COBOL-word mapping is applied (open kb/Work/PB1383, which claims DOC-A.1-68). A second defect, proposed new: an AS-phrase externalized name with leading or trailing spaces can never be reached. ProgramRegistry registers the literal verbatim ('trail  '), while every CALL, CANCEL and ADDRESS OF PROGRAM target is Trim()'d before the case-insensitive match, so even CALL "trail  " fails with EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND (probe /tmp/adj/doc/doc-w1-s3/probe/as68b.cob; the leading-space form is as68c.cob). The arm a) mapping is sound: the externalized name is the program-name spelling, or the AS literal's content, matched case-insensitively. EXTERNAL data names map the same way (EXT1 = ext1, AS "Shared Two" = AS "shared two"), and AS "" is refused with COBOLNET1794 (x68.cob, as68.cob). But the row cannot state a formation rule for AS literals until the space handling is fixed.
